title: Count Even and Odd
directAnswer: Keep two counters. For each element, increment `even` when `x % 2 == 0`, otherwise `odd`.

rules: odd = n − even if you want one counter.
remember.takeaway: Counting categories is one pass with one counter per category.
remember.formula: for x: if x%2==0 even++ else odd++
whenToUse: Bucketing elements into a few categories

problemStatement: Given an integer array `nums`, return how many elements are even and how many are odd, as a pair `[evenCount, oddCount]`.
understanding: One pass: test each element's parity and bump the matching counter.

approaches.name: Two counters
approaches.whenToMention: This is the standard, expected solution — lead with it.
approaches.explanation:
Classify each element by parity and tally it: this is the **classify-and-count** pattern with one counter per category.

**Why test `% 2 == 0`.** As in even-or-odd, `%` can be negative in Java/C++ (`-3 % 2 == -1`), so detecting odd via `== 1` misclassifies negative odds. Test evenness with `== 0` and treat the else branch as odd.

**Why two counters (or one).** Two counters read clearly. You *can* keep just an even counter and compute `odd = n − even` at the end, since every element is exactly one or the other — a nice space micro-optimisation worth mentioning.

**Order of the result.** Return `[even, odd]` in the agreed order; swapping them is a silent correctness bug the tests will catch.
hints: One pass, classify each element, bump a counter.
Use `% 2 == 0` for even so negatives are handled.
You could track only evens and derive odds as n − even.
approaches.complexityReasoning: one parity test and one increment per element.

dryRun.intro: Bump the matching counter per element.

pitfalls: Returning the counts in the wrong order.

commonMistakes: Testing `x % 2 == 1` for odd — fails on negative odds.
